title: Everyone Quotes the Ford Pinto Memo. It Was Not About the Pinto, and the Jury Never Saw It.
description:
More like this already exist: this is one of 56 full-length cases on this channel, 28 of them posted in the last 28 days.
More are finished and already scheduled. Subscribing is what puts the next one in front of you:
https://www.youtube.com/@primedocumentarystudio?sub_confirmation=1

On 28 May 1972 Lilly Gray set out from Anaheim for Barstow in a six-month-old Ford Pinto with her neighbour, thirteen-year-old Richard Grimshaw. The carburettor float had saturated with fuel; the Pinto stalled and coasted to a halt in the middle lane of the freeway, and a car behind struck it. Mrs Gray died a few days later. Grimshaw survived, the court wrote, only through heroic medical measures. A jury awarded Richard Grimshaw $2,841,000 in compensatory damages and $125 million in punitive damages. The Gray family received $659,680 in compensatory damages. The trial judge cut the punitive award to $3.5 million as the price of denying a new trial, and in 1981 the California Court of Appeal affirmed.

That opinion is where most of what people know about this car comes from. Because Ford was appealing a verdict against it, the court viewed the evidence in the light most favourable to the parties who had won below. On that footing it found a rush project in which styling preceded engineering; a tank behind the rear axle with only 9 or 10 inches of crush space, far less than in any other American car; crash tests showing the fuel system could not meet a proposed 20-mile-per-hour standard; and results that went up the chain to the officials who decided to go into production. At an April 1971 product review meeting executives received a report, exhibit 125, recording that a design cost saving of $10.9 million could be realised by delay. That was the evidence of conscious disregard, and it was admitted.

The memo everyone quotes was not. "Fatalities Associated with Crash-Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires", by E. S. Grush and C. S. Saunby, was excluded from evidence in that trial. It was not an internal ledger of Pinto crashes but an attachment to a petition Ford filed with the federal regulator in September 1973, and its own text says the analysis concerns the static rollover requirement proposed for FMVSS 301. Its cost table is a rollover analysis counting 11 million cars and 1.5 million light trucks across the entire American industry for a year, not one company's models. The word Pinto appears nowhere in it. And the $200,000 per fatality was not Ford's price for a life: it was the regulator's own figure, and the memo says so twice.

In September 1977 Mother Jones published Mark Dowie's article. Ford waited eight years, it said, because an internal cost-benefit analysis that places a dollar value on human life said it was not profitable to make the changes sooner, and the table argued against an $11-per-car improvement that would prevent 180 fiery deaths a year. The $11 was the industry-wide rollover figure. The appellate court's own figure for a package of rear-impact fixes was $15.30 a car — a different number, from a different document, about a different requirement. Two sentences earlier, the same article reported correctly that the $200,000 came from a 1972 government study.

In May 1978 the regulator made an initial determination that the fuel system was defective and set a hearing for 14 June. Ford recalled first: campaign 78V143000, 1,400,000 vehicles, 1971-1976 Pintos and 1975-1976 Mercury Bobcats, a longer filler pipe and a polyethylene shield. That August three young women died when their Pinto was struck from behind in Indiana, and an Elkhart County grand jury indicted Ford Motor Company itself, deliberately charging no individual, on three counts of reckless homicide and one of criminal recklessness. Maximum penalties: $36,000 in fines. It could have indicted individual executives and chose to charge only the company. After a ten-week trial in Winamac, Indiana, the jury found Ford not guilty.

None of this is a defence of the car. The regulator, compiling reports from several sources including Ford, identified 38 instances of rear-end impact on a Pinto producing fuel-tank leakage or fire: 27 deaths and 24 non-fatal burn injuries; the magazine's figure of 500 burn deaths, possibly 900, was its own estimate and carried no source. In the study that assembled those numbers the Pinto's overall fatality rate sat among its competitors, its rear-impact fire rate was above several of them, and it flunked crash tests the Chevrolet Vega passed. What the record will not support is the sentence everybody remembers.

Some imagery in this film is AI-assisted and symbolic; no real-person likeness is shown, no real vehicle, badge or document is reproduced, and no crash, fire or injury is depicted.
Grimshaw v. Ford Motor Co., 119 Cal. App. 3d 757 (1981). NHTSA recall campaign 78V143000. E. S. Grush & C. S. Saunby, "Fatalities Associated with Crash-Induced Fuel Leakage and Fires" (Ford, 1973). Mark Dowie, "Pinto Madness", Mother Jones, Sept./Oct. 1977. Gary T. Schwartz, "The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case" (1991).
